interactive.title: The gear board
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in fifteen small screens on a gear board. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it. Each screen sets out its own gears on pegs, already meshed. One gear is the driver. It has a ring round its rim to drag, or you can turn it with the arrow keys. Everything it meshes with turns with it. Each gear shows its tooth count at its centre, one marked tooth on its rim and an arrow for the way it turns. On a puzzle, only the driver's arrow shows until you check your answer. Some boards have two counters at a mesh, one for each gear. They tick up as teeth pass. Each tooth on one gear pushes one tooth on the other past the mesh. So the two counters at a mesh always match. At the mesh, the teeth of both gears move the same way. So the two gears turn opposite ways. Each mesh flips the direction, so the arrows alternate along a line. Some boards close the gears into a loop. An even loop turns. In an odd loop, the last gear and the first both try to turn the same way. So the loop locks, and the mesh that closes it is drawn in red. Try to turn a locked loop's driver and the gears rock a hair and the red mesh pulses, but nothing goes round. The counters give the speed rule too. A gear passes its own tooth count each time it turns once. So the teeth it passes in a minute are its speed × its teeth. The two counters at a mesh match, so n₁T₁ = n₂T₂. Here n is a gear's speed in rev/min and T its number of teeth. On a typed puzzle, Why? appears once you have checked an answer. The screens, in order. Screen 1, do, Which way: a 12-tooth driver meshes with a 20-tooth gear, and nothing moves yet. "The driver turns clockwise. Which way will the 20-tooth gear turn?" Choices: Clockwise, Anticlockwise (right). Hint: "Watch where the two gears touch. The teeth there must move together." Why: at the mesh, the driver's right-hand teeth move down. They push the 20-tooth gear's left-hand teeth down too. Teeth moving down on its left side turn it anticlockwise. After Check the pair turns. Screen 2, show, Teeth pass one for one: the same pair, with a small ink arrow at the mesh and two counters below it. Words: "Where two gears mesh, each tooth pushes one tooth on the other gear. So at the mesh, the teeth of both gears move the same way. The driver's right-hand teeth move down. They push the next gear's left-hand teeth down, and that turns it anticlockwise." Then "Turn the driver by its rim." Read: the 12-tooth driver turns clockwise and the 20-tooth gear turns anticlockwise. An arrow at the mesh shows the teeth of both gears moving down together. The two counters at the mesh always show the same count. Screen 3, do, Five in a line: five gears in a line, still, labelled 1st to 5th on one line under the row. "The first gear turns clockwise. Which way does the fifth turn?" Choices: Clockwise (right), Anticlockwise. Hint: "Each mesh flips the direction. Count the meshes." Why: five gears make four meshes, so there are four flips: anticlockwise, clockwise, anticlockwise, clockwise. So the fifth turns the driver's way. After Check the line turns. Screen 4, do, Mixed sizes: four gears in a line with 12, 40, 16 and 30 teeth, the driver clockwise. "Which way does the fourth gear turn?" Choices: Clockwise, Anticlockwise (right). Hint on Clockwise: "Size changes the speed, not the direction. Count the meshes." Why: three meshes make three flips, so the fourth turns anticlockwise. The big 40-tooth gear turns slower, but it still flips the direction once. Screen 5, do, A bent chain: six equal gears zigzag across the board, the driver at the left end and the last gear at the right. "Six gears zigzag across the board. The driver turns clockwise. Which way does the last gear turn?" Choices: Clockwise, Anticlockwise (right). Hint: "The bends change nothing. Count the meshes." Why: six gears make five meshes, so there are five flips. Five flips leave the last gear turning anticlockwise, against the driver. Where the gears sit makes no difference. Screen 6, show, Odd and even: lines of two, three, four and five gears turn side by side. Words: "Each mesh flips the direction, so the arrows alternate along a line. An odd number of gears turns the last one the driver's way. An even number turns it the other way." Read: the same three sentences. Screen 7, show, Close the loop: a triangle of three gears, each meshing with the other two, locked, with its last mesh in red; beside it a ring of four gears turning. Words: "Close three gears into a triangle, and the third meets the first. Both try to turn the same way. So their teeth at that mesh would have to move opposite ways. Neither can give way, so the triangle locks." Read: the triangle of three is locked, its last mesh drawn in red, and the ring of four turns. Trying to turn the triangle's driver only rocks it a hair and pulses the red mesh. Screen 8, do, Which loop turns: three loops lying flat on the board, of five, six and seven gears. "Which loop turns?" Choices, in a row that wraps at phone width: The loop of five, The loop of six (right), The loop of seven. Hint: "Round a loop the directions alternate. The last gear must end up opposite the first." Why: six is even, so the sixth gear turns opposite to the first, as their mesh needs. Five and seven are odd, so those loops lock, whatever the gears' sizes. Screen 9, show, Count the teeth: a 12-tooth driver meshes with a 36-tooth gear, with the mesh counters and each gear's revolution counter. Words: "Each tooth that passes on one gear pushes one past on the other. Three turns of the 12-tooth driver pass 36 teeth. That is one turn of the 36-tooth gear. A gear passes its own tooth count every turn. So its teeth a minute are speed × teeth, the same on both gears: n₁T₁ = n₂T₂. Here n is the speed in rev/min and T the number of teeth." Read: three turns of the 12-tooth driver pass 36 teeth and turn the 36-tooth gear once. Screen 10, do, typed, How fast: "A 12-tooth gear turns at 60 rev/min and drives a 36-tooth gear. How fast does the 36-tooth gear turn?" A typed answer: 20 rev/min, a whole number. Slips: 180 rev/min, "That makes the bigger gear faster. It has more teeth to take in, so it turns slower."; 3 rev/min, "That is the ratio, 36 ÷ 12. Divide the speed by it." Hint: "Work out the teeth a minute through the mesh first." Why: 60 × 12 = 720 teeth a minute pass the mesh. Then 720 ÷ 36 = 20 rev/min. The 36-tooth gear's speed shows "?" until the answer is checked. Screen 11, show, The idler: a 20-tooth gear arrives between the 12-tooth driver and the 36-tooth gear. The 36-tooth gear's arrow and speed fade in with it. Words: "Put a 20-tooth gear between the two. Now 60 × 12 = 720 teeth a minute pass each mesh. So the last gear still turns at 20 rev/min, but now the driver's way. The middle gear is called an idler gear." Read: a 20-tooth idler sits between them and turns at 36 rev/min. The 36-tooth gear still turns at 20 rev/min, now the driver's way. Screen 12, do, typed, Through an idler: "A 15-tooth gear at 1200 rev/min drives a 40-tooth idler. The idler drives a 45-tooth gear. How fast does the 45-tooth gear turn?" A typed answer: 400 rev/min, a whole number. Slips: 450 rev/min, "That is the idler's speed. It passes the same teeth a minute on to the last gear."; 3600 rev/min, "That makes the bigger gear faster. Turn the ratio the other way up." Hint: "The idler passes on the driver's teeth a minute." Why: 1200 × 15 = 18,000 teeth a minute pass both meshes. Then 18,000 ÷ 45 = 400 rev/min. The idler only flips the direction. Screen 13, do, typed, The drum: "A motor turns an 18-tooth gear at 1440 rev/min. It drives a 72-tooth gear on a drum. How fast does the drum turn?" A typed answer: 360 rev/min, a whole number. Slips: 5760 rev/min, "That makes the drum faster than the motor. The 72-tooth gear has more teeth to take in."; 4 rev/min, "That is the ratio, 72 ÷ 18. Divide the speed by it." Hint: "Teeth a minute first, then divide by the drum gear's teeth." Why: 1440 × 18 = 25,920 teeth a minute. Then 25,920 ÷ 72 = 360 rev/min. Screen 14, do, typed, How many teeth: "A 24-tooth gear turns at 300 rev/min. The gear it drives must turn at 100 rev/min. How many teeth does that gear need?" A typed answer: 72 teeth, a whole number. Slip: 8 teeth, "That gear would turn faster than the driver. A slower gear needs more teeth." Hint: "The teeth a minute are the same on both gears." Why: 300 × 24 = 7200 teeth a minute. Then 7200 ÷ 100 = 72 teeth. Screen 15, do, Add a fifth: a ring of four gears turning, with a spare gear in a tray below it. "You fit a fifth gear into the ring. What happens when you turn the driver?" Choices, in a row that wraps at phone width: It still turns; It locks (right); It turns, but slower. Hint on It still turns: "Count the gears in the ring now." Hint on It turns, but slower: "A gear of the same size cannot slow the ring. Count the gears in it now." Why: five is odd. So round the ring, the fifth gear and the first both try to turn the same way. Nothing moves, whatever the sizes. After Check the fifth gear drops in and the new mesh goes red.
interactive.ignores: The gears are drawn rigid, with teeth that fit perfectly and never slip. Real gears have a little play between their teeth. So a locked loop may rock slightly, but it still cannot turn. The board turns as fast as you drag. So a speed in rev/min comes from a puzzle's numbers, not from your finger. The red mesh is just the one closed last. The lock belongs to the whole loop. Every gear lies flat in one plane with its teeth on the outside. A ring gear has its teeth on the inside, and it turns the same way as a gear meshing inside it. Bevel gears meet at an angle, and they follow other direction rules too. While the axles stay put, speed × teeth is the same on both sides of every kind of mesh. In an epicyclic gearbox, some axles ride round. Then the rule holds only for speeds measured against the arm that carries them.

explain.text:
Where two gears mesh, their teeth pass one for one. So neighbouring gears turn opposite ways, and both pass the same number of teeth a minute. The point where two gears meet is their [[mesh]]. Each tooth on the driver pushes a tooth on the other gear along with it. So at the mesh, the teeth of both gears move the same way. That turns the two gears opposite ways.[^1] Say the driver turns clockwise, with the next gear on its right. The driver's right-hand teeth move down. They push the next gear's left-hand teeth down too. That turns it anticlockwise.

So each mesh between outside teeth flips the direction. In a line of such gears, each one meshes with the next. So the directions alternate along the line. An odd number of gears in a line turns the last one the driver's way. An even number turns it the other way. A gear's size changes how fast it turns, not which way. One gear set between two others makes them turn the same way. It is called an [[idler gear]]. Now close a line into a loop, so the last gear meshes with the first. With an even number of gears, the last turns opposite to the first. That is what their mesh needs, so the loop turns. With an odd number, the last gear and the first try to turn the same way. At their mesh, the teeth would have to move in opposite directions. Neither gear can give way. An odd number of gears in a closed loop in one plane will not turn, whatever their sizes and tooth counts.[^2]

The same count gives the speed. In any minute, both gears pass the same number of teeth through the mesh. A gear passes its whole tooth count each time it turns once. So the teeth it passes in a minute are its speed in rev/min × its number of teeth. Call the speed n and the number of teeth T. Then n₁T₁ = n₂T₂ for any two meshed gears whose axles stay put.[^3] A 12-tooth driver at 60 rev/min passes 60 × 12 = 720 teeth a minute. A 36-tooth gear takes in those 720 teeth, so it turns at 720 ÷ 36 = 20 rev/min. Turn the ratio upside down and you get 60 × 36 ÷ 12 = 180 rev/min. That cannot be right, because the bigger gear has three times as many teeth to take in. An idler passes on the same 720 teeth a minute, whatever its size. So it changes the output's direction, not its speed.

In a winch, a small gear on the fast motor drives a gear with many more teeth on the drum. So the drum turns far slower than the motor. The slower gear also turns harder. That is where the winch's extra pull comes from. **Meshed gears pass teeth one for one, so neighbours turn opposite ways. Speed × teeth is the same on both: n₁T₁ = n₂T₂.**

analogy.text: A loaded transformer balances its ampere-turns: I₁N₁ = I₂N₂. So the winding with more turns carries less current. A gear pair balances speed × teeth the same way: n₁T₁ = n₂T₂. So the gear with more teeth turns slower.
analogy.breaks: The transformer's balance is only nearly true, because the primary also carries a small magnetising current. The gear count is exact, since every tooth that passes the mesh is counted on both gears. A transformer's polarity depends on how its windings are wound and connected. A mesh between outside teeth always reverses the direction.

practice.text:
- Before you turn a machine's gears by hand, isolate it and lock it off. Make sure no hanging load or spring can turn it. Keep fingers clear of any mesh that can move.
- Number the gears from the driver, and note which gear meshes with which.
- Direction: flip it at every mesh between outside teeth. Take a simple line, with one gear to each axle. An odd number of gears turns the last one the driver's way. An even number turns it the other way.
- Loops: count the gears in any closed loop. An odd number lying flat in one plane locks.
- Speed: work out the teeth a minute through the first mesh, the driver's speed × its teeth. In a simple line, divide that by each gear's teeth to get its speed.

**Rule of thumb:** the gear with more teeth turns slower than its partner. An idler flips the direction and leaves the output speed alone.

**Worked example:** a 20-tooth gear on a motor at 1450 rev/min drives a 25-tooth idler. The idler drives a 100-tooth gear. Teeth a minute: 1450 × 20 = 29,000. The idler turns at 29,000 ÷ 25 = 1160 rev/min. The output turns at 29,000 ÷ 100 = 290 rev/min. There are three gears in a line, so the output turns the motor's way.

**Common mistakes**
- Thinking meshed gears turn the same way. With outside teeth, their teeth move together at the mesh. So the gears turn opposite ways.
- Turning the ratio upside down, so the bigger gear comes out faster.
- Letting the idler's teeth change the output speed. It passes on the same teeth a minute.
- Letting a gear's size decide its direction. Count the meshes instead.
- Missing an odd loop. Three gears that all mesh with each other cannot turn.

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the two counters at a mesh ticking up together, tooth for tooth, as the two gears turn opposite ways, when you turn the driver by its rim.

checks.label: Where gears meet, the teeth of both move the same way, so the gears turn opposite ways: true at every mesh that turns, on every screen
An odd number of gears in a closed loop in a plane will not turn, whatever their size and tooth count: every odd loop drawn locks, every even one turns, and an odd loop of mixed sizes locks too
When gear 1 and gear 2 are in mesh, N1 × Z1 = N2 × Z2: speed × teeth is the same on both sides of every mesh drawn with speeds, so the idler screen shows 60, 36 and 20 rev/min

Both counters at a mesh always match: two turns of the 12-tooth driver pass 24 teeth on each side, three turns pass 36 and turn the 36-tooth gear once, and the idler passes on the same count at both its meshes

Each mesh flips the direction: the 20-tooth gear turns against the driver, the fifth of five in a line turns the driver's way, the fourth of four and the sixth of a bent chain the other way, every row follows odd and even, only the loop of six turns, and a fifth gear locks the ring
Each typed answer and slip is worked from speed × teeth: 20 rev/min (slips 180 and 3), 400 rev/min (450 and 3600), 360 rev/min (5760 and 4) and 72 teeth (8), and the board draws the same
Before an answer nothing gives it away: an unknown speed reads "?", the idler's speed and the new gear stay hidden, and only the drivers show their way round; after it, the answer is drawn
Every mesh is drawn with its gears touching at their pitch circles, every loop closes tooth in gap, and gears that do not mesh never touch
Every demonstration is over within 4.5 s of its screen opening and nothing moves during the 0.35 s screen fade; every answer's motion is over within 2.5 s

applied.problem: "Each mesh flips the direction" and "n₁T₁ = n₂T₂ for any two meshed gears" are stated too widely: a ring gear's inside mesh does not flip, a compound pair on one shaft does not mesh, and in an epicyclic box with moving axles absolute speeds break the rule.

Dividing the first mesh's teeth a minute by every gear's teeth, and the gear-count parity rule, fail for compound trains (next lesson); the safety step misses a hanging load back-driving a winch; "meshed gears turn opposite ways" fails for ring gears.
"Speed × teeth is the same on both sides of every kind of mesh" is false for absolute speeds in an epicyclic gearbox, where planet axles ride round; it holds only while the axles stay put.
